cases.abstract: FlashAttention-2 addresses execution costs that persist after exact attention avoids quadratic intermediate storage in GPU memory. Scalar normalization, insufficient parallel work, and exchanges of partial outputs between warps can still limit throughput. The method postpones normalization, schedules sequence blocks independently, and assigns query rows to separate warps so that forward outputs need no cross-warp reduction. It preserves attention without approximation and retains auxiliary storage linear in sequence length. Across attention benchmarks on an A100 80GB SXM4 GPU, it is 1.7-3.0 times faster than FlashAttention and 3-10 times faster than standard PyTorch attention. End-to-end training on eight such GPUs yields smaller, context-dependent gains: for a 1.3B-parameter GPT-style model, throughput rises from 170 to 220 TFLOPs/s per GPU at an 8k context, versus 189 to 196 at 2k. For multi-query decoding, the bottleneck shifts to loading the KV cache. Distributing this loading across thread blocks achieves attention-kernel speedups of up to seven times over FasterTransformer on an A100 80GB GPU. Kernel gains therefore translate unevenly to whole-model training, while decoding benefits from parallelizing a different memory bottleneck.
cases.methods: The forward pass of FlashAttention-2 reduces normalization work by maintaining an unnormalized attention output for each query block. For every key/value tile, it tracks a running row maximum, an exponential sum, and a value-weighted numerator. When a tile raises the maximum, the accumulated sum and numerator are rescaled by the exponential of the old maximum minus the new one before adding the tile's contributions. The numerator is divided by the sum only after all tiles have been processed. This preserves full-row softmax without repeatedly dividing partial outputs, reducing scalar arithmetic that cannot exploit the GPU's fast matrix-multiplication units. Saving each row's final logsumexp lets the backward pass reconstruct probabilities from recomputed score tiles instead of storing the complete attention matrix. The operation therefore changes how exact attention is executed and stored, not its quadratic arithmetic cost; auxiliary storage remains linear in sequence length.
cases.results: FlashAttention-2 improves whole-model training throughput most at longer contexts in the reported runs, rather than reproducing its kernel speedup uniformly. On eight A100 80GB SXM4 GPUs, the 1.3B-parameter GPT-style model rises from 189 to 196 TFLOPs/s per GPU at a 2k context when FlashAttention is replaced, but from 170 to 220 at 8k. The 2.7B-parameter model similarly reaches 225 TFLOPs/s per GPU at 8k, versus 175 with FlashAttention. The modest 2k gain and larger 8k gain are consistent with attention becoming a more consequential part of training as context grows. These training rates count the full causal attention matrix under the paper's FLOPs convention, whereas kernel benchmarks halve attention FLOPs for causal masking; their utilization figures are not interchangeable. In the fixed-total-token kernel benchmarks, standard PyTorch attention runs out of memory at 16k while FlashAttention-2 still runs. That comparison validates retaining the storage benefit of tiled attention, not a new memory advantage over FlashAttention.
cases.notes: The revision keeps the normalization mechanism and separates kernel speed from end-to-end benefit. Algorithm 1 supports deferred normalization and linear auxiliary storage; Table 1 supports the context comparison, and Figure 4 supports the 16k memory outcome. Table 1 gives 220/72, approximately 3.06, for the largest ratio to the no-FlashAttention baseline, whereas the body states a 2.8-fold maximum; the passages avoid that unresolved maximum. The training FLOPs convention counts full causal attention. H100-specific optimization and automatic block tuning remain future work, not measured gains.

cases.abstract: Speculative decoding replaces some serial Transformer evaluations with concurrent checks of tokens generated by a cheaper proposal model. The target model scores the proposed continuations in parallel; probability-ratio acceptance and residual resampling retain exactly its sampling distribution, regardless of the proposal model. No target retraining is required. The central tradeoff is that more guesses can produce more tokens per target evaluation but also add proposal cost and waste arithmetic after rejection. The analysis predicts walltime gains from distributional overlap and relative proposal latency, assuming independent, identically distributed acceptance rates, sufficiently long generations, and enough capacity for concurrent target evaluations without extra walltime. With existing T5 checkpoints at batch size one on a single TPU-v4, a 77M-parameter T5-small proposal accelerates 11B-parameter T5-XXL English-German translation by 2.6 times under standard sampling and 3.4 times under greedy decoding, compared with ordinary autoregressive decoding. Summarization gains are 2.3 and 3.1 times, respectively. Larger proposals accept more guesses yet deliver smaller speedups. Acceptance is therefore insufficient to choose a proposal model: its evaluation cost also determines the latency benefit.
cases.methods: Speculative decoding accepts a proposed token x with probability min(1, p(x)/q(x)), where p and q are conditional distributions adjusted for the chosen sampling rule. Accepted proposals contribute mass min(p(x), q(x)); sampling from the normalized positive part of p - q after rejection supplies the remaining target mass. This restores the target distribution even when the proposal is inaccurate. A cheaper model generates gamma guesses sequentially; the target then verifies their conditional distributions concurrently. The first rejection discards later guesses and triggers residual resampling; if all guesses pass, an extra token is drawn directly from the target. Each iteration therefore produces one to gamma + 1 tokens. With i.i.d. acceptance rates of mean alpha, the expected count is 1 + alpha + ... + alpha^gamma. Dividing by 1 + gamma*c predicts long-generation speedup, where c is relative proposal latency, provided concurrent target evaluations cost no more walltime than one ordinary evaluation.
cases.results: The T5 results show why acceptance alone is an incomplete predictor of latency. In English-German translation with an 11B-parameter T5-XXL target, T5-small and T5-large achieve 2.6-fold and 1.4-fold speedups over ordinary autoregressive decoding under standard sampling at batch size one on a single TPU-v4. Acceptance rises from 0.62 to 0.71 with the larger proposal, yet higher overlap does not make it faster. The runs also use seven and three guesses, respectively, so they compare complete decoding configurations rather than isolate proposal size. T5-small performs better under greedy decoding, reaching 0.75 acceptance and a 3.4-fold speedup. Its summarization gains are lower, at 2.3-fold under standard sampling and 3.1-fold under greedy decoding. Together, these comparisons support selecting proposals by useful tokens per unit time rather than distributional overlap alone. Faster generation need not mean less arithmetic: rejected guesses waste computation, and acceleration requires spare capacity for concurrent verification.
cases.notes: Preserved the exact-sampling argument and the proposal-cost comparison rather than treating higher acceptance as a speed guarantee. Sections 2.3 and 3.3 distinguish unconditional distributional correctness from conditional runtime analysis. Table 2 supports measured T5 walltime gains; proposal size and guess count differ in the standard-sampling comparison. Section 4.2 reports acceptance, not measured walltime acceleration, for GPT-like and LaMDA models. Equal output distributions do not imply identical sampled sequences, and latency improvements do not establish fewer arithmetic operations.
